title: Why a job's location still matters in attracting talent: Data
gist: Drawing on BCG's Cities of Choice survey of ~17,000 professionals in 80+ cities, the piece argues that the density of urban amenities is negatively correlated with job satisfaction while the perceived improvement trajectory of daily-life experience is strongly positive — a 30-point job-satisfaction gap between high- and low-experience cities. The named winners are not London, Paris or Tokyo but Dubai, Bengaluru, Kuala Lumpur, Riyadh, Baku and New York, making urban experiential quality a corporate site-selection variable rather than a lifestyle footnote.

insights.claim: In BCG's Cities of Choice survey, the correlation between a city's experiential density (bars, restaurants, concerts, museums per head) and worker job satisfaction is negative, not positive — amenity counts are a misleading site-selection metric.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Location scorecards and city-ranking indices built on amenity counts are measuring the wrong variable; discount rankings that lead with 'number of restaurants/museums'.
insights.quote: the relationship between experiential density (number of bars, restaurants, concerts, museums etc.) and job satisfaction is negative

insights.claim: What predicts worker satisfaction is whether residents feel their city is getting better — especially in entertainment, leisure and everyday life — making the rate of change, not the stock of amenities, the leading indicator of a city's talent pull.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Screen candidate metros on improvement momentum (new public space, transit, nightlife, walkability) rather than absolute endowment — a second-derivative framework that favors mid-tier cities.
insights.locator: The cities with the most amenities are not

insights.claim: The 'experience dividend' is defined as the talent advantage a company gains by locating in cities where residents feel the daily experience of using amenities is improving — an explicitly perception-based, survey-measurable variable rather than an infrastructure count.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Gives a named, quantifiable construct that HR, real-estate and site-selection teams can add to location models alongside cost and incentives.

insights.claim: Established world capitals such as London, Paris and Tokyo have the largest amenity inventories but deliver worse day-to-day usability because congestion, cost, distance, stress and friction degrade the experience of consuming those amenities.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Friction — not scarcity — is the binding constraint in superstar cities, so investments that cut congestion and cost may buy more talent retention than new cultural assets.
insights.quote: Congestion, cost, distance, stress and friction get in the way.
insights.locator: These usual suspects may have the most restaurants

insights.claim: 78% of workers say they like their jobs in cities where residents are satisfied with the experiential quality of daily life, versus only 48% in cities where they are not — a 30-percentage-point spread attributable to city experience.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A 30-point swing in job satisfaction is large enough to move attrition and hiring costs materially; it is a quantified argument for weighting city choice heavily in workforce planning.
insights.quote: In cities where residents are satisfied with the experiential quality of daily life, 78% of workers say they like their jobs. In cities where residents are not satisfied, only 48% do

insights.claim: Across 11 tested dimensions of city life, the experiential dimension ranked essentially tied with economic opportunity for impact on job satisfaction and outranked housing, healthcare, transportation and safety.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Experience competes with jobs themselves as a driver of satisfaction — a ranking that inverts the usual policy hierarchy where housing and transit dominate the talent-attraction debate.
insights.quote: The experiential dimension came in essentially tied with economic opportunity. It outranked housing, healthcare, transportation and safety.
insights.locator: We tested 11 aspects of city life

insights.claim: The findings rest on a survey of nearly 17,000 professionals across more than 80 cities on five continents, which separately measures amenity density and the lived experience of using those amenities.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Sample scale and the density-vs-experience split make this a usable evidence base for challenging incumbent city rankings in board-level location debates.
insights.locator: To better understand this, we draw on BCG’s

insights.claim: Workers in high-experience cities are 12 percentage points more likely to say they plan to stay where they are, making urban experiential quality a direct retention lever.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Retention economics can be modelled against city choice; a 12-point stay-intent delta translates into measurable turnover-cost savings for large employers.
insights.locator: This experience dividend is especially powerful for retention.

insights.claim: The retention gap between high- and low-experience cities is 20 points for workers under 25 but only six points for workers in their late 50s — the effect is concentrated in exactly the young talent pool employers compete hardest for.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Firms dependent on early-career hiring pipelines face a >3x sharper location penalty than those with older workforces; graduate-heavy sectors should reweight city choice accordingly.
insights.quote: For workers under 25, the retention gap between high- and low-experience cities is 20 points. Among workers in their late 50s, it is just six points.
insights.locator: The effect is even larger among younger workers.

themes.theme: Breadth: income, GDP and sector controls

insights.claim: Moving to a higher-performing city has roughly the same effect on job satisfaction as moving up an income bracket, implying compensation alone cannot offset a poor city experience.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Pay premiums used to hold staff in low-experience locations are an inefficient substitute; the trade-off can be priced against relocation or satellite-office costs.
insights.quote: Moving to a higher-performing city has roughly the same effect on job satisfaction as moving up an income bracket

insights.claim: The experience dividend survives controlling for GDP per worker, so it is not simply a proxy for city wealth — poorer but improving cities can out-compete richer stagnant ones for talent.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Opens emerging-market metros as credible talent hubs on merit rather than cost arbitrage alone — relevant to offshoring and capability-centre siting.
insights.locator: When we controlled for gross domestic product per worker

insights.claim: In information technology — the sector most able to work remotely — the job-satisfaction gap between high- and low-experience cities is still 20 points, showing remote flexibility does not neutralize the location effect.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'geography is dead for tech' thesis; tech employers cannot rely on distributed work to escape a weak host-city experience.
insights.locator: In information technology, the gap between high-

insights.claim: The dividend holds across every income level and every sector tested, from manufacturing to healthcare to agriculture — it is not confined to knowledge work or high earners.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Widens applicability to industrial and frontline-labour siting decisions, not just white-collar HQ placement.
insights.locator: What's more, the dividend runs through every sector

themes.theme: Where the dividend is compounding: risers over superstars

insights.claim: The cities identified as already capturing the experience dividend are Dubai, Bengaluru, Kuala Lumpur, New York City, Riyadh and Baku — a list dominated by Gulf and Asian risers rather than traditional Western capitals.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A concrete watchlist for talent-hub expansion and for real-estate/urban-amenity exposure; New York is the sole legacy superstar to make the cut.
insights.quote: Cities doing this well include Dubai in the United Arab Emirates, Bengaluru in India, Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia, New York City in the United States, Riyadh in Saudi Arabia and Baku in Azerbaijan.
insights.locator: That signal points to a different group of cities

insights.claim: The authors argue these winning cities have been overlooked by companies, implying an information asymmetry that early movers on site selection can arbitrage before wage and property costs reprice.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: First-mover advantage in these metros is framed as time-limited; watch office absorption and corporate capability-centre announcements in Riyadh, Baku and Kuala Lumpur as confirmation.
insights.quote: places many companies have overlooked but where the experience dividend is already taking shape
insights.locator: That signal points to a different group of cities

themes.theme: Implications for corporate siting and city budgets

insights.claim: Remote and hybrid work have increased rather than decreased the importance of location, because workers now have the flexibility and power to choose where they build their lives — shifting part of the talent equation outside the firm's control.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Employers lose leverage over pay/culture as sole retention tools; city quality becomes a competitive input the firm must select for rather than build.
insights.locator: Remote and hybrid work have also heightened

insights.claim: Companies still evaluate location on cost, logistics, incentives and existing prestige, none of which answer the operative question of where people will want to stay — a stated gap in standard site-selection practice.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Adds a fifth screen — improving experiential quality — to conventional location models; a checkable question to put to any relocation or expansion proposal.
insights.quote: where will people want to stay?
insights.locator: For companies, the experience dividend changes

insights.claim: For cities, parks, public space, culture, nightlife, walkability and street life should be reclassified from post-development lifestyle extras into core economic development spending, because experience retains talent, talent draws companies, and companies draw investment and capital.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Implies a reallocation of municipal budgets and a rationale for financing quality-of-life infrastructure — relevant to muni credit narratives and urban-amenity development pipelines.
insights.quote: Investing in the experience of daily life is not a luxury.
insights.locator: For cities, the experience dividend matters even more.

insights.claim: The authors' implied causal chain runs experience to talent retention to corporate location to capital inflows, positioning quality-of-life spending as an upstream driver of city investment attraction rather than a consequence of it.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Reverses the conventional sequencing used in city investment pitches; watch whether cities pursuing this ordering (Riyadh, Dubai) show faster corporate footprint growth.
insights.quote: the experience of the city is what retains talent and a deep, stable pool of talent is what draws companies, investment and capital
insights.locator: However, the experience of the city is what retains talent
